learningObjectives: Know how and when to use Conditions.

elements.text: You want to validate that a green car is automatic and a blue one is manual. If both validations sit in the same TestStep, the TestCase would try to check for BOTH transmissions at once — and always fail, since a single car can't have two competing validations.

Conditions solve this: they tell Tosca to apply a validation (or any TestStep/Folder/Value) ONLY when a specific prerequisite is met — e.g., verify the green success message only when a positive quantity was entered, and skip it when a negative one was.

elements.term: Three levels Conditions can be set on
elements.description: Conditions instruct Tosca when to use — or skip — certain elements:
items: TestStepFolder level — the rule applies to running the ENTIRE folder's contents.
TestStep level — applies to that one TestStep.
TestStepValue level — applies to just that specific Value.

elements.text: Using Conditions well means only ONE Template is needed to cover multiple paths — instead of maintaining several near-duplicate Templates by hand. Changes only need to be made in one place, and they apply automatically to every generated TestCase.

elements.title: Add a Condition
items: Make the Condition column visible via the column chooser.
Drag and drop the relevant Instance from the TestSheet onto the Template's Condition cell for that TestStepFolder/TestStep/TestStepValue.
By default, the logical statement shown is == (equal to).

rows: The element must equal this value for Tosca to run the TestStep.
Instance must be 'Valid' for this TestStep to run.
Not equal to / everything except — runs for every value EXCEPT the one specified.
'Take the exam' != 'Teacher' → only students take the exam.
ALL listed conditions must be met.
Used when multiple conditions must simultaneously hold.
ANY ONE of the listed conditions must be met (Tosca's default when combining 2+ conditions).
Avoid stacking many ORs — it gets hard to read/maintain.

elements.text: Real example from the Payment Process Template: 'Workflow.Payment Method.Credit Card' != "No Credit Card used" runs the TestStep for ANY credit card used, using a single != condition instead of one OR per card type — far more business-readable.

Prefer != over stacking many OR conditions. Piling up several OR layers to cover 'everything except X' makes the Condition set hard to read and maintain — a single != achieves the same result more simply.

How to tell if an element already has a Condition set: check whether its icon has changed in the Navigation pane — Tosca visually marks TestStepFolders, TestSteps, and TestStepValues that carry a Condition, so you don't have to open each one to check.

elements.title: Final steps
items: Use Check Template to catch any errors in the newly added Conditions/links.
You now have a complete, working set of TestCases ready for testing.

examPitfalls.title: Overusing OR conditions instead of !=
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Candidates stack many OR conditions to express 'run for everything except this one value', producing a long, unreadable Condition set.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use the != operator to express 'run for everything except X' in one simple, business-readable condition, instead of many ORs.

examPitfalls.title: Setting a Condition at the wrong level
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Learners set a Condition on a whole TestStepFolder when they only meant to gate a single Value (or vice versa), unintentionally skipping unrelated steps.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Match the Condition level to its intended scope: TestStepFolder gates the whole folder's contents; TestStepValue gates just that one value.

examPitfalls.title: Forgetting the two post-modification steps
examPitfalls.trapDescription: After adding Conditions, candidates run the TestCases without first validating and refreshing them.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Always run Check Template, then Re-Instantiate, after any Template modification — including adding Conditions.

examPitfalls.title: Not knowing how to spot an existing Condition
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Candidates open every TestStepFolder/TestStep/TestStepValue one by one to check whether a Condition was already set.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Tosca changes the icon of any element that carries a Condition — glance at the Navigation pane instead of opening each element individually.

examPitfalls.title: A trailing space in the Property Name breaks the match
examPitfalls.trapDescription: When setting up a verification TestStepValue (e.g. for 'Wrong Password' or 'Wrong Email Error'), typing the property name with an invisible trailing space — "InnerText " instead of "InnerText" — makes ScratchBook fail with 'The property "InnerText " was not found.', even though the name looks correct at a glance.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: If a Verify TestStepValue fails with 'The property "X" was not found', re-type the property Name field from scratch instead of trusting what's visually there — a stray leading/trailing space is invisible but breaks the exact-string match Tosca uses to look up the property on the scanned Module.

practiceQuiz.scenario: At which THREE levels can Conditions be set in a Template? (choose the option listing all three correctly)

options.text: TestStepFolder, TestStep, and TestStepValue level.
ExecutionList, RequirementSet, and TestSheet level.
Attribute, Instance, and Module level.
Only at the TestCase level.

practiceQuiz.hint: These are the three levels of granularity inside a Template.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Conditions can be set at TestStepFolder level (gates the whole folder), TestStep level, or TestStepValue level (gates just that value).

practiceQuiz.scenario: You want a TestStep to run for every credit card type EXCEPT when no card is used at all. Which is the best-practice Condition?

options.text: A chain of OR conditions, one per specific credit card brand.
No condition is needed; all TestSteps always run.
'Payment Method.Credit Card' == "Visa" OR == "MasterCard" OR == "Amex" (and so on for every card).
'Payment Method.Credit Card' != "No Credit Card used"

practiceQuiz.hint: A single != is simpler and more business-readable than many ORs.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Using != lets you express 'run for anything except this one case' in a single, readable condition, avoiding a long chain of OR statements for every possible card type.

practiceQuiz.scenario: When multiple Conditions are added to the same TestStep, what logical statement does Tosca apply by default?

options.text: NOT — none of the conditions may be true.
AND — all conditions must be true.
OR — only one of the conditions needs to be true.
XOR — exactly one condition must be true, no more.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's the more permissive of the two common logical operators.
practiceQuiz.rationale: By default, Tosca sets the logical statement to OR when more than one condition is added to a TestStep — meaning any single one of them being true is enough.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What must be visible in the Template grid before you can set a Condition, and how do you add it?

options.text: The XL Reference column, enabled from the Property tab.
The RequirementSet column — enable it via Execution settings.
No column needs to be enabled; Conditions are set via a separate dialog only.
The Condition column — enable it via the column chooser.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's a standard Tosca grid customization step.
practiceQuiz.rationale: You must first make the Condition column visible via the column chooser before you can drag and drop Instances into it.

practiceQuiz.scenario: After adding new Conditions to a Template, what two steps should you do before the TestCases are ready to use?

options.text: Convert the Template back to a TestCase, then reconvert it.
Run Check Template, then Re-Instantiate.
Nothing further is required; Conditions apply immediately without Instantiation.
Delete the TestSheet, then create a new one.

practiceQuiz.hint: Same 2-step pattern used after any Template modification.
practiceQuiz.rationale: As with any Template change, you must Check Template to catch errors, then Re-Instantiate so the Conditions actually take effect in the generated TestCases.

practiceQuiz.scenario: How can you quickly tell whether a TestStepFolder, TestStep, or TestStepValue already has a Condition set, without opening each one individually?

options.text: Its icon changes in the Navigation pane.
There is no visual indicator; you must open each element to check.
Its font turns bold automatically.
Tosca sends a notification for every Condition set.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's a visual, at-a-glance indicator in the tree, not a popup or text change.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Tosca changes the icon of any TestStepFolder, TestStep, or TestStepValue that carries a Condition, so you can spot conditioned elements directly in the Navigation pane without opening each one.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Verify TestStepValue fails in the ScratchBook with the Loginfo: 'The property "InnerText " was not found.' The Name field visually looks correct. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Condition column is not visible.
The TestStepValue's ActionMode should be 'Input' instead of 'Verify'.
An invisible leading or trailing space in the property Name field, breaking the exact-string match.
The Module was never scanned and doesn't exist at all.

practiceQuiz.hint: Notice the space right before the closing quote in the error message itself.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Tosca matches property names as exact strings. A stray space (like 'InnerText ' instead of 'InnerText') is invisible in the UI but causes an exact 'property not found' error — retype the Name field from scratch to fix it.

quickRecap.value: Let ONE Template cover multiple test paths without competing/contradictory validations.
Show Condition column (column chooser) → drag & drop Instance from TestSheet.
Default operator — element must equal the value.
Not equal to / everything except — avoids stacking many ORs.
AND = all must be true; OR = any one is enough (Tosca's default for 2+ conditions).
The element's icon changes in the Navigation pane — no need to open each one.
Often an invisible trailing/leading space in the Name field — retype it instead of trusting how it looks.
